strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing algorithm discovery benchmarks (MLE-Bench, MLGymBench, etc.) are small, manually curated, and lack a principled meta-train/meta-test separation. Transplanting procedural content generation principles from deep RL (Contextual MDPs, unsupervised environment design) to algorithm discovery tasks is a sensible and well-motivated framing, and the paper clearly articulates the structural flaws of prior suites (Section 3).

The submitted system is substantial: 10 task domains spanning supervised to RL settings, modular editable/fixed components, a two-stage meta-train/meta-test generation process to limit leakage, and a containerised evaluation harness. The example task walkthrough (Section 4.1) and Appendix F give enough implementation detail to understand how tasks are actually built.

The empirical work is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: three open-source models evaluated on DiscoBench Single and All, an 'until success' ablation, a full sweep of all 15 On-Policy RL module combinations (Appendix G), success@3 analysis (Appendix L), per-task breakdowns (Appendix M), and a prompt-optimisation case study showing a monotonic meta-test improvement with the number of optimisation tasks (Ktasks=30 Elo 1071 vs 957 for Ktasks=1, with non-overlapping CIs).

The paper is transparent about its limitations: low success rates are openly reported, the contamination risk from publication is acknowledged with a concrete mitigation (private API-based DiscoBench), the compute/cost budget is disclosed (23k GPU-hours, ~$1200 API cost), and the impact statement is one of the more thoughtful ones I have seen, including discussion of misuse, labour effects, and why domain-scoped optimisation is safer than generalist optimisation.

The code is released open-source, all prompts and task descriptions are provided (Appendices N and O), and the authors verified that domains run on consumer-grade hardware, supporting reproducibility and accessibility.
weaknesses: The headline 'millions of tasks' claim (Ntasks = 493M) is largely combinatorial inflation. Tasks differ only in which subset of d datasets is assigned to meta-train/meta-test/excluded, which of m modules is editable, and backend/evaluation choices. Many combinations are semantically near-identical (e.g., CIFAR-10 plus one of four similar datasets), so the effective diversity is far smaller than the advertised count. The redundancy analysis partially acknowledges this (mean Spearman ~0.4), but the task-count framing is overstated.

The core diversity evidence is statistically weak. The Spearman rank correlations in Appendices I and M are computed over rankings of essentially 4 items (3 models + baseline) per task, derived from only 3 seeds per model. Rank correlations over 4 items are extremely noisy, and the observation that meta-test correlation structure 'dissolves to noise' (Figure 3b) is equally consistent with low statistical power as with genuine semantic diversity. The diversity conclusions should be hedged much more carefully.

No agent consistently beats the fixed baseline on Elo (Table 2), success rates are low (11-34% on DiscoBench All), and DiscoBench All confidence intervals are very wide (e.g., 533 [-183, 700]). This is honestly reported and framed as headroom, but it also means the benchmark's discriminative power above the 'all fixed' baseline is not yet well established, and much of the signal currently comes from failure modes (syntax errors, hardcoding) rather than algorithmic quality.

The evaluation is limited to one ADA scaffold (MLGym) and three open-source models; no frontier models are tested, and there is no comparison against results on existing benchmarks (e.g., how the same models fare on MLE-Bench or MLGymBench), making it hard to situate DiscoBench difficulty and to verify the claimed evaluation advantages in practice.

The prompt-optimisation case study is only run once per Ktasks setting with 30 optimisation steps, and meta-train results are non-monotonic (Ktasks=5 > Ktasks=10), so the central monotonic trend claim rests on a single trajectory per condition without error bars over optimisation seeds.

Meta-train/meta-test dataset splits are fixed across all tasks within a domain (Appendix H). This is convenient but means agents see the same datasets repeatedly across optimisation, which partly undermines the 'millions of distinct problems' narrative and could bias discovered algorithms toward particular dataset families; the paper does not analyse this fixed-split choice.

Some presentation issues: occasional typos ('module combinations with the with the same dataset splits'), heavy reliance on the appendix for core analyses (redundancy, per-task results), and the Elo methodology's failure-penalty scheme is somewhat ad hoc and only sketched in the main text.

strengths: The core idea of applying procedural generation to algorithm discovery tasks is well-motivated and the related-work positioning (Section 3's critique of MLE-Bench/MLGymBench, poor evaluation, contamination, saturation) is thorough and largely convincing.

The system itself is substantial: ten domains spanning RL, supervised learning, continual learning, unlearning, etc., with a well-defined task interface (editable modules, meta-train/meta-test splits, initialisations, evaluation types), and the meta-train/meta-test distinction genuinely addresses a real evaluation flaw in existing suites.

The paper is transparent about experimental limitations: low success rates, tasks omitted from 'until success' analysis, compute/cost reporting (Appendix E.4), and honest discussion of contamination risk for the released DiscoBench.
Appendices are unusually comprehensive: per-task results, module-combination sweeps, redundancy analysis, prompts, and derived task-count formulas support reproducibility of the setup.

The module-difficulty sweep (Appendix G, Table 8) provides a concrete, useful empirical finding: adding editable modules consistently lowers success rates, and the paper is honest that the 'higher performance ceiling' claim cannot be confirmed due to zero success at 3-4 modules.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim of the paper — that optimising ADAs over more procedurally sampled tasks improves performance (Section 7, Table 3) — rests on a single agent scaffold, a single ADA LLM, 30 optimisation steps, and four K_tasks settings with overlapping or wide confidence intervals. Meta-train results are explicitly non-monotonic (K=5 beats K=10), and the 'clear monotonic trend' is really only supported by the K=1 vs K=30 comparison. This is thin evidence for what the abstract positions as a key demonstration of DiscoGen's value.

The redundancy analysis (Appendix I, Figure 3) is interpreted as evidence of 'semantic diversity', but it is equally consistent with the meta-test evaluation being dominated by noise: if rank correlations dissolve to random noise when only the datasets change, either algorithms truly do not transfer, or per-dataset performance measurements are too high-variance to be reliable. The paper does not disentangle these possibilities, which undercuts both the diversity claim and the meaningfulness of meta-test Elo scores.

The headline '>400 million tasks' figure is a combinatorial count of configuration tuples (Eq. 1). Most configurations differ trivially (e.g., same module set with one different dataset), and the paper provides no evidence that task variation within a domain produces meaningfully different discovery problems beyond the module-count/difficulty sweep in one domain.

Evaluation results are sobering and not adequately leveraged: no ADA consistently beats the 'all fixed' baseline in Elo, success rates are low (11-34% on DiscoBench All), and Appendix K's evidence of 'novel discoveries' consists of two hand-selected algorithms, one of which (AM-Softmax for language modelling with conflicting label-smoothing/entropy objectives) is more plausibly a lucky/overfit artifact than an interesting algorithm. The paper needs systematic analysis of discovered-algorithm quality, not anecdote.

The Elo methodology (Appendix E.2) with a failure penalty, three-seed aggregation, and bootstrap CIs is ad hoc and conflates success rate with quality; combined with the Until-Success analysis that omits the hardest tasks (On/Off-Policy RL train, Model Unlearning loss), headline meta-train/meta-test comparisons are hard to interpret across settings.

DiscoBench tasks are not yet public and the eventual evaluation plan (private API benchmark) is aspirational; as submitted, independent verification of the benchmark's key properties (contamination resistance, transfer structure) is not possible, and reproducibility of the paper's experiments depends on released artefacts whose exact configuration (pseudo-random splits, per-task hyperparameters) is only partially specified.

The meta-train/meta-test split design has a confound the paper does not address: 'very long-to-run datasets are reserved for meta-testing' (Section 5.1), so meta-test datasets are systematically harder/more expensive, which plausibly explains the observed meta-train-to-meta-test performance drop (Section 5.2) independently of any genuine generalisation deficit. This weakens the paper's central methodological selling point.

DiscoBench All results have extremely wide confidence intervals (e.g., GPT-OSS 533 [-183, 700]) due to low success counts, yet these numbers are tabulated as if comparable; the paper should aggregate or exclude rather than present unstable Elo estimates.

Significance is real but prospective: Sections 6 and 8 are largely a research agenda. The paper would be substantially stronger with one more rigorous experiment (e.g., RL-trained or evolved ADA over many tasks showing measurable gains on held-out tasks) rather than prompt tuning as the sole case study.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-argued gap: existing algorithm discovery benchmarks (MLE-Bench, MLGymBench, etc.) are small, manually curated, lack a proper meta-train/meta-test split, and are prone to contamination. The diagnosis in Section 3 is convincing and clearly connected to the design of DiscoGen.

The procedural generation framework is well designed: tasks are specified by a small configuration file, editable/fixed modules give combinatorial task diversity, and the two-stage task creation (meta-test codebase built only after the meta-loop) is a sensible mechanism to limit test leakage. The task count derivation in Appendix F.2 is transparent and reproducible.

DiscoGen covers an impressively broad range of ML subfields (supervised, RL, continual learning, unlearning, UED, etc.), with detailed per-domain documentation in the appendix, and the code is released open-source, which is important for community uptake.

The experimental setup is unusually well documented: hyperparameters, Elo methodology with derivation, bootstrap CIs, action budgets, per-task breakdowns, compute/cost reporting, and Success@3 analysis to show tasks are not simply unsolvable. The honest treatment of failures (agents underperform the baseline Elo even with three successful attempts) strengthens credibility.

The prompt-optimisation case study provides a concrete demonstration that the generator produces useful optimisation signal, with an intuitive finding (prompts optimised over more diverse tasks generalise better), and the example discovered algorithms in Appendix K show genuinely interesting, non-baseline artefacts.

The impact statement is thoughtful and unusually substantive, addressing safety framing (specialist vs generalist optimisation), misuse, labour-market and environmental concerns, and the AI-safety-relevant Model Unlearning domain.
weaknesses: The empirical validation of the framework's core promise is relatively thin. The main evidence that DiscoGen improves ADAs is a single prompt-optimisation experiment (30 steps, one ADA, one prompt-optimiser model, seemingly no repetitions over the optimisation run itself), which limits the strength of the Ktasks trend claim given the acknowledged noise in Elo and prompt search.

The claim of 'millions of tasks' is inflated by combinatorial counting over module/dataset/initialisation subsets; the effective diversity is much smaller (10 analysed domains, 49 modules, median 59,622 nominal tasks). The rank-correlation analysis (mean Spearman ~0.4) is a reasonable start but the diversity claim would be stronger with fewer tasks and richer semantic variation, or with evidence from actual ADA optimisation across many tasks.

Only the 'performance' evaluation type is used despite three being supported, and only 'empty' initialisation is tested; the claims about energy/time objectives and baseline-initialisation modes are unvalidated. This weakens the breadth of what is demonstrated versus what is described.

The Elo methodology is ad hoc: models are penalised for failed runs relative to baselines (failure penalty does not apply to baseline comparisons), which can distort cross-model comparisons, and there is an unexplained anomaly where the baseline dramatically outperforms all agents in DiscoBench All (Elo 1409 vs ~1184 max) that is noted but not fully analysed. Selection effects (Until Success analysis omits hardest tasks) further complicate interpretation.

Several design choices may confound meta-train/meta-test distinctions in practice: e.g., the LibriBrain meta-train/meta-test splits come from the same participant/chapters, and some domains have very few datasets (Continual Learning has 1 meta-train dataset), so 'generalisation' being tested may be weaker than framed.

Success rates are very low in DiscoBench All (11-34%), and the paper relies partly on Success@3 and extrapolation to argue optimisation signal exists; direct evidence of stable ADA optimisation (e.g., weight updates or repeated prompt-optimisation seeds) is not provided.
The research directions in Section 6 are largely speculative and占 a substantial portion of the paper; the only executed demonstration beyond evaluation is the prompt-optimisation case study.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated critique of existing ADA benchmarks (lack of meta-train/meta-test separation, contamination, small task sets), with a principled procedural-generation framing borrowed from PCG in RL.

Substantial engineering effort and scale: 14 task domains spanning diverse ML subfields, ~35,000 GPU-hours of experiments, three open-source models evaluated across DiscoBench Single/All with three meta-seeds, and an existence proof that all tasks are solvable.

Thorough, honest evaluation: the paper reports low success rates and that agents rarely beat the all-fixed baseline (Appendix I.2), analyses meta-train/meta-test rank correlation to show task diversity and meta-overfitting, and includes Success@3 and 'until success' analyses to disentangle robustness from skill.

Useful ablations demonstrating the generator's controllability: difficulty scales smoothly with number of editable modules (Figure 2), and empty vs baseline initialisations measurably change difficulty (Section 8.2).

The prompt-optimisation scaling experiment (Section 7) is a genuine, if modest, demonstration of the ADA optimisation loop, including an interesting held-out-domain result that conventional meta-train evaluation would have misrepresented performance.
Good reproducibility posture: open-source release, hyperparameters, prompts, Elo computation details, compute/cost reporting, and a detailed appendix describing all domains, datasets and splits.
weaknesses: The headline claim of '~100B' tasks is largely a combinatorial count of dataset/module/backend reconfigurations; the paper does not convincingly establish that these tasks are semantically distinct discoveries rather than rearrangements of existing codebases and public datasets. Many codebases (PureJaxRL, PPO, Boax, ReBRAC) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR, OGBench) are well represented in pre-training, weakening the contamination-resistance argument.

The central selling point — enabling ADA optimisation/training — is demonstrated only via prompt tuning with a single optimisation run per K_tasks, 30 iterations, and no statistical treatment (no seeds/error bars over optimisation runs). The meta-train column in Table 4 is non-monotonic and differences are within wide confidence intervals, so the scaling trend rests on fairly weak evidence.

A concerning result is left somewhat under-analysed: even with three successful attempts, no agent consistently outperforms the fixed baseline on meta-test (Appendix I.2). This raises questions about whether the benchmark's reward signal currently provides meaningful optimisation signal for building better ADAs, beyond penalising failures.

The Elo methodology is unconventional (penalising failed runs, pairwise comparisons among only ~4 competitors), and although the 'until success' analysis mitigates this, the main tables conflate robustness and solution quality; several All-Edit confidence intervals are very wide, making model comparisons hard to support.

Practical accessibility and reproducibility gaps: DiscoBench is not yet public ('planned private API'), evaluation types other than performance are claimed but not exercised, and several experiments are restricted to small subsets due to compute limits (single model for initialisation ablation, few domains for prompt tuning).

Some structural aspects of the meta-train/meta-test split feel weak: e.g., Brain Speech Detection meta-test is chapters of the same participant/book, and CV meta-train (MNIST/CIFAR10) is far easier than meta-test (StanfordCars/TinyImageNet), so dataset-shift confounds algorithm-transfer measurements.
Section 6 research proposals are speculative and occupy considerable space relative to the demonstrated results; the paper would benefit from a sharper focus on what was actually validated.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing ADA benchmarks (MLE-Bench, MLGym-Bench, etc.) are small, manually curated, and conflate algorithm development with evaluation; the meta-train/meta-test separation proposed here is a principled fix supported by the rank-correlation analysis in Appendix F showing that task rankings dissolve when datasets change.

The procedural-generation framing is well-motivated and carefully executed: 14 domains spanning diverse ML subfields, a clear task specification interface (Example 1), two-stage task construction to reduce meta-test leakage, and containerised execution to prevent evaluation hacking.

Unusually thorough empirical reporting: Elo with bootstrap CIs, success rates and Success@3, per-task breakdowns (Appendix J), ablations over editable-module count (Fig. 2) and initialisation type, plus a scaling experiment (Table 4) showing prompt-optimisation gains increase with task count, including on held-out domains.
Honest limitations discussion: the authors openly report that ADAs rarely beat the fixed baseline and that conclusions for All Edit are difficult at current success rates, rather than overselling.

Good reproducibility: open-source release, all prompts in the appendix, explicit hyperparameters, Elo methodology, and compute/cost details (~35k GPU-hours, ~$1600 API spend). The impact statement is substantive and non-boilerplate.
weaknesses: The headline 'billions of tasks' claim is inflated relative to the demonstrated utility. The count is a combinatorial bound over dataset/module/backend/evaluation configurations, but diversity within a domain is bounded by a handful of datasets and modules (median 59k tasks; several domains have under 10k). The rank-correlation analysis partially addresses this, but the paper does not show that scaling tasks beyond the ~60 sampled in the optimisation loop actually helps.

The empirical demonstration of DiscoGen's core promise is modest. The central use case — ADA optimisation — is shown only via prompt tuning with a single optimizer model (Claude 4.5 Sonnet) and a single ADA (MLGym with DeepSeek-V3.2) over 30 updates. The optimisation loop is expensive and high-variance, and Table 4 reports only one run per K_tasks setting, so the monotonic trend (especially in the narrow held-out set) could plausibly be noise. No weight-based or scaffold-based optimisation is attempted.

Results show the benchmark may be poorly calibrated for its stated purpose: agents frequently fail to even reproduce well-known baselines, and even 'until success' Elo (Table 7) never exceeds the all-fixed baseline. The paper frames this as headroom for ADAs, but it also raises the concern that 'discovery' tasks in Single Edit reduce mostly to reimplementing known algorithms, and that the empty-initialisation difficulty axis may limit optimisation signal.

Contamination-resistance claims are only partially convincing. All codebases (PureJaxRL/CleanRL PPO, ReBRAC, modded-nanogpt, OpenUnlearning) and most datasets are public and plausibly in pretraining corpora; Table 1's own 'partial' marking is apt. The claim rests on the meta-test split and on evaluation predating publication, with the private-API plan deferred to future work.

The All-Edit comparisons are statistically weak (very wide bootstrap CIs, e.g., 595 [142, 758] for GPT-OSS), and the paper itself concedes conclusions there are 'difficult' — yet All Edit is one of the main advertised axes of task variation.

Novelty is moderate rather than fundamental: the contribution is an application of established PCG/UED principles (Cobbe, Matthews, Nikulin) to a new domain, plus benchmark engineering. The research-direction proposals in Section 6 are aspirational and largely untested.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated contribution: applying procedural generation principles from RL (Contextual MDPs / UED) to algorithm discovery tasks addresses genuine structural flaws in existing ADA benchmarks (no meta-train/meta-test separation, contamination risk, manual-curation-limited scale). The framing and terminology (inner-loop / meta-loop / ADA optimisation loop) is clearly defined.

The two-stage task generation process (meta-train codebase built before the agent starts; meta-test codebase created only after the meta-loop, with non-editable files overwritten) is a thoughtful, concrete mechanism for reducing test leakage and evaluation hacking, going beyond what MLE-Bench or MLGym-Bench provide.

Comprehensive experimental treatment: three open-weight models on a fixed agent scaffold, Elo ratings with bootstrap CIs, success@3 and 'until success' analyses, ablations over module combinations (Fig. 2), initialisation types (Sec. 8.2), and a demonstration use-case (prompt optimisation scaling with K_tasks, including held-out domains).

Honest reporting: the paper openly acknowledges that the all-fixed baseline outperforms all agents in Elo, that All-Edit conclusions are hard to draw due to low success rates, and that prompt tuning is a limited form of optimisation. Per-task results are exhaustively reported in the appendix.

Good reproducibility and transparency: open-source release, prompts included (Appendix K), hyperparameters, compute (~35k GPU-hours, H200s) and API cost (~$1600) documented; accessibility on consumer hardware noted. Thorough impact statement covering misuse, labour, and democratisation considerations.
weaknesses: The diversity claims rest on statistically fragile evidence. The Spearman rank correlations are computed over only four entities (three models plus the fixed baseline) per dataset, which makes rank correlations extremely noisy at such small sample sizes. The observation that meta-test correlation structure 'dissolves to noise' (Appendix F) is interpreted as evidence of semantic diversity, but it is equally consistent with rank noise from ~3 seeds; no significance testing is provided to disentangle these.

The '~100B tasks' headline is combinatorial accounting rather than a demonstration of semantic diversity. Many 'datasets' within a domain are near-duplicates (e.g., seven LibriBrain splits from a single participant listening to chapters of Sherlock Holmes; eleven standard synthetic BO functions), so the effective diversity of meta-train/meta-test splits is likely far smaller than the headline number suggests.

The central ADA evaluation uses only three open-weight models on a single agent scaffold (MLGym). Conclusions about the current ADA capability ceiling, meta-overfitting, and the usefulness of DiscoBench as a benchmark would be stronger with a frontier or closed model and at least one alternative scaffold, as prior benchmark papers (e.g., MLE-Bench) did.

The prompt-optimisation experiment (Sec. 7) has limited statistical support: a single optimisation run per K_tasks setting, Elo differences between adjacent K_tasks values within overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., K=5 vs K=10 meta-test), and non-monotonic success rates. The claimed 'positive relationship' between task count and performance is suggestive but not firmly established; variance over optimisation seeds is not reported.

The failure-penalty scheme in the Elo calculation (models with more successful runs dominate those with fewer) is somewhat ad hoc and interacts with the success-rate differences across models; while the 'until success' analysis helps, the headline Table 3 numbers embed this design choice.

DiscoBench is described as 'not yet public' with plans for a private API, which limits immediate reproducibility of the evaluation for the community, and the mitigation of contamination (fixed splits selected pseudo-randomly, long-running datasets reserved for meta-test) is only partially justified.
